doc.title: Kidd Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

chapter: New Orleans families, lifestyle and retirement
title: Music appreciation classes, Katrina and retirement
summary: Teaching music appreciation, finding students related to Bechet and Picou, and retiring when Katrina closed the music department.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Well and that’s what I want it to do. And you know the main thing about it, there’s some people I see say, “man, you still teaching school? If I had all the years you had I’d have been retired a long time ago. I say, “man I enjoy what I’m doing.” I didn’t go to school to sell insurance. I haven’t practiced all my life to sell cars. I didn’t do this to sit in an office and be an executive now. I’m doing it, exactly what I wanted to do. And if Katrina hadn’t come along I wouldn’t have retired. They took the music department away. And they wanted me to teach four classes of music appreciation. So you know the music appreciation people, they don’t want to be there themselves, that’s just cause the university, you’ve got to take a class in music. You understand? And I used to have one class, and you know I tried to bring up all the music like we talk about now and so forth. And believe it or not they had a lot, every semester in my class they would have somebody who had some famous person in their family and didn’t even know them. Like I remember Sidney Bechet’s people coming around. I say how the hell? I say man you don’t know how great this man is? I say they got a statue of this man in Paris. Say what? You mean to tell me — you know, and both kinds. And what’s that other old man, oh man there’s a famous old clarinet player, played on “High Society” who was that? Picou. Alphonse Picou. Man, they had people and Picou I said man I was with Picou three weeks before he died. I said that old man was playing when a cast on his arm. Say what? I say y’all just don’t know how famous he was. You know what I’m talking about? So I used to use that, say all right, give me the names of the people, let me see who’s got somebody, who’s your cousin? I found a cousin or a grandfather or something in one of my classes. I said you didn’t mean to tell me you didn’t know that? And then I would take it and bring them up to that and bring them up to Coltrane and Charlie Parker and bring them to all the classical composers that they didn’t hardly ever hear ‘cause nobody ever played them, and play it for them in class. And you see all of this is the way the music developed you know? So that’s how I dealt with that but I really didn’t like it to a certain extent, it was just one class. But you tell me to teach four classes of music appreciation, you know, and well all the instruments went under water, and anything that we had, so that the institution said it would be a while before they get it back up and we were teaching in trailers, so we didn’t have a band, in a trailer teaching a band, if we had it was going to be hard, so they cut the music department out completely. So that’s when I retired. But I would probably be there now. And I say it when I feel like quitting I was going to quit. ‘Cause I was enjoying what I was doing.
